prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. I moved from Autor, Dorn and Hanson to this set between my opening ballot and round 1, and I used the exchange to test that move rather than to settle into it. The achievement answers a first-order question: who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand, and how persistent and place-specific the adjustment is. It combines a conceptual account of skill demand and the education-technology race with transparent local-labour-market evidence on import competition. These findings have been replicated, extended and contested for roughly a decade or more, and the contest has refined magnitudes and persistence more than it has overturned the qualitative results. On the chair's question about Katz, as I understand the literature (not independently verified here): his citable contribution is the long-run account of relative skill demand and supply, the Katz-Murphy lineage and the education-versus-technology work. That account is the setting in which the trade-shock results are read as one source of labour-demand shifts among several. It is a distinct strand from the China-shock identification and does not derive from the task papers. Autor ties the two strands together. Hanson anchors the trade-shock evidence. A citation worded around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, and not around the task model as a theory, limits the overlap with Acemoglu's 2024 recognition and leaves Levy and Murnane unclaimed. If the committee decides the achievement is only import competition and local adjustment, I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a citation narrowed to match: 'for showing how import competition reshapes local labour markets'. I would rank that below the joint version. A two-name Autor-Hanson award is the weakest of the three for me. It leaves out Dorn from the trade-shock papers and Katz from the skills strand, so it credits neither strand cleanly.
statement.case_against: Attribution under the three-name cap remains the strongest reservation. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is excluded, and the task framework has contributors outside the credited names. The joint citation can be read as two prize-sized strands combined through Autor, and my own wording cannot fully answer that reading. The size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects remain debated, and some of the evidence is specific to the US episode. The 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes on labour, education and technology themes may reduce the marginal case. As a trade and industrial-organisation economist who works on price adjustment, I may weigh the transparency of identification more heavily than conceptual novelty. I also cannot rule out that my preference for B027 over B006 or B012 reflects my empirical-micro orientation rather than the relative importance of the work.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He regards the collateral-amplification mechanism as the cleanest attribution on the list. He says he cannot resolve the Katz-Dorn choice on the evidence and would accept B027 if the committee finds a coherent citation.
responses.response: I agree that B006 has the cleanest attribution of the macro candidates, and that omitting Gertler is defensible if the citation is written around the collateral mechanism and not the accelerator. I would not treat B006 as a weak candidate. My remaining difference is about how much weight to give directly examined evidence relative to a clean originator pair. The Katz-Dorn question is a choice about the scope of the citation, not a disagreement about merit. For a joint technology-and-trade citation I would use 'for showing how technological change and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets'. For a narrower version I would use 'for showing how import competition reshapes local labour markets'. If no coherent B027 citation can be agreed, I am genuinely unsure between B006 and B012. B006 is better on attribution, and B012 is better on long empirical confirmation. I have moved B006 into my alternatives for that reason.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file names Autor, Hanson and Katz for B027. He moved from B012 because the technology and trade strands share the question of where labour-demand adjustment lands. He treats Dorn's omission and the Acemoglu overlap as the main costs.
responses.response: I take your round-1 position as it is now, not your opening two-name proposal, and on that basis we hold the same configuration for similar reasons. Your earlier question about whether the shock papers are a conceptual advance or strong applied work is the one I most want to answer. The advance is the combination of a framework for why demand shifts and designs that show where and how slowly adjustment happens. That is why I think the work is more than applied, and why I put Katz on the skills side of that combination. I also take your point about B012. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum and the 2008 prize do make its credit more crowded. That is part of why I keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred part, even though it is closer to my own field.

responses.point: Enflo moved from Autor, Dorn and Hanson to Autor, Hanson and Katz. She argues that wording the citation around labour demand and adjustment, and not the task model, lets one citation hold. She says that if the citation narrows to import competition, Dorn should replace Katz.
responses.response: We have followed the same path and reached the same position on both versions. Your point about wording matters to me more than the choice of name. A citation that does not claim theoretical priority for the task framework avoids the overlap with Acemoglu and the missing credit to Levy and Murnane. I would add one condition. The words 'labour demand' and 'wages' have to be backed by the skill-demand strand, and that is the reason Katz is in the set. If the committee uses your wording and still excludes Katz, the citation claims more than the credited names support. I would then prefer the narrow version with Dorn.

responses.point: Teorell prefers Katz to Dorn so that the citation covers technology and skills as well as import competition. He concedes that Dorn's claim on the trade-shock papers is at least as strong as Hanson's. He would support the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio if the committee decides the citation is narrowly about trade exposure.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning and with the concession. The test I would apply is whether each credited name is most responsible for a central finding that the citation names. For the joint citation, Autor, Hanson and Katz pass that test and Dorn is a real exclusion. For the narrow citation, Autor, Dorn and Hanson pass, and Katz is the one left out. I do not think the committee should treat the two trios as interchangeable, because they imply different achievements. I also share your reluctance to read the opening support as evidence of merit. The people who share the joint configuration reached it partly through attribution arguments, and the committee should test those arguments directly and not rely on the count.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats technology and trade as one achievement or two, which decides between the joint trio (Autor, Hanson, Katz) and the narrow trio (Autor, Dorn, Hanson).
How much the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes, and Acemoglu's parallel task work, reduce the distinct increment of the Autor-Katz skills framework.
How robust the size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects are beyond the US episode.
Whether B006 or B012 is the better fallback if no coherent B027 citation can be agreed. I am unsure, because B006 is better on attribution and B012 is better on long empirical confirmation.
My assessments of Katz's and Dorn's roles rest on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 files, and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. My research on price adjustment, exchange-rate pass-through and invoicing currency is adjacent to B012 and B010, my alternative B012 in particular, though not to my preferred B027 or my other alternative B006. My co-author list includes Chad Syverson (Chicago Booth), who is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a former Swedish prime minister. This is a public fact and no bearing on any shortlisted candidate is apparent from the supplied profile. None of the credited names in my preferred configuration or alternatives appears among my listed co-authors. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated, and no recusal is assumed.
